claims.evidence: This is stated as background for the splicing experiments.

claims.claim: SKIP, another component of the NTC, has a lengthened circadian period when mutated.
claims.source: Like MAC3A and MAC3B, another component of the NTC, SNW/SKI-interacting protein (SKIP), has a lengthened circadian period when mutated, likely due in part to the dysregulation of PRR9 and PRR7 splicing (Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform PRR9a.
claims.source: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant we observe a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform, termed PRR9a, as well a secondary inactive form, referred to as PRR9b (Figure 11A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11A-B.

claims.claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is a decrease in the amplitude of the inactive PRR9 spliceoform PRR9b.
claims.source: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant we observe a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform, termed PRR9a, as well a secondary inactive form, referred to as PRR9b (Figure 11A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11A-B.

claims.claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is an increase in the average amplitude of the inactive spliceoform PRR9c, which retains an intron inappropriately.
claims.source: This is accompanied by an increase in the average amplitude of the inactive spliceoform, PRR9c, which retains an intron inappropriately (Figure 11C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11C.

claims.claim: Accurate expression of genes involved in the circadian clock is essential to maintaining 24 hr periodicity.
claims.source: Accurate expression of genes involved in the circadian clock is essential to maintaining 24 hr periodicity (Más et al., 2003; Rawat et al., 2011; Somers et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Constitutive expression of full-length MAC3B causes period lengthening similar to mac3a/mac3b double mutant.
claims.source: Interestingly, constitutive expression of the full-length MAC3B causes period lengthening similar to mac3a/mac3b double mutant (Figure 12).
claims.evidence: This is a result from circadian period measurements shown in Figure 12.

claims.claim: Maintaining proper expression of MAC3B is necessary for clock function.
claims.source: This indicates that maintaining proper expression of MAC3B is necessary for clock function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the overexpression data.

claims.claim: F-box decoy proteins are able to interact with target proteins and regulatory partners and retain the ability to form biologically relevant complexes.
claims.source: We have previously shown that F-box decoy proteins are able to interact with target proteins and regulatory partners and retain the ability to form biologically relevant complexes (Lee et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Five known components of the plant NTC were identified in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides.
claims.source: We compared this list to the previously identified components of the plant NTC, and identified five common components in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides, three of which (MAC3A, CELL DIVISION CYCLE 5 (CDC5), and MODIFIER OF SNC1,4 (MOS4)) were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls (Table 4) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments shown in Table 4.

claims.claim: MAC3A, CDC5, and MOS4 were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls.
claims.source: We compared this list to the previously identified components of the plant NTC, and identified five common components in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides, three of which (MAC3A, CELL DIVISION CYCLE 5 (CDC5), and MODIFIER OF SNC1,4 (MOS4)) were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls (Table 4) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments shown in Table 4.

claims.claim: The MAC3B decoy is capable of forming biologically relevant complexes in vivo.
claims.source: This data suggests that the MAC3B decoy is capable of forming biologically relevant complexes in vivo and importantly supports the idea that the decoy strategy can be used for genetic and biochemical analyses of E3 ligase function in plants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the IP-MS data.

claims.claim: MAC3A and MAC3B were observed interacting in the IP/MS data.
claims.source: We observed MAC3A and MAC3B interacting in our IP/MS data and PRP19, the MAC3A and MAC3B orthologue from yeast and humans, is predicted to form a tetramer (Grillari et al., 2005; Ohi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments with citations.

claims.claim: PRP19 is predicted to form a tetramer.
claims.source: We observed MAC3A and MAC3B interacting in our IP/MS data and PRP19, the MAC3A and MAC3B orthologue from yeast and humans, is predicted to form a tetramer (Grillari et al., 2005; Ohi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Tetramer formation of PRP19 is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil.
claims.source: Tetramer formation is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil that is present in MAC3A and MAC3B (Li et al., 2018), and was included in our MAC3A and MAC3B decoy constructs (Figure 12).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 12.

claims.claim: The conserved coiled coil is present in MAC3A and MAC3B.
claims.source: Tetramer formation is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil that is present in MAC3A and MAC3B (Li et al., 2018), and was included in our MAC3A and MAC3B decoy constructs (Figure 12).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Constitutive expression of the MAC3B WD domain causes two subpopulations of transgenic plants, one with lengthened period (25.5 hr) and one with shortened period (22.5 hr).
claims.source: Constitutive expression of the MAC3B WD domain causes two subpopulations of transgenic plants, one with lengthened period (25.5 hr) and one with shortened period (22.5 hr) (Figure 12).
claims.evidence: This is a result from circadian period measurements shown in Figure 12.

claims.claim: The MAC3B WD phenotype more closely resembles the MAC3A decoy phenotype.
claims.source: Interestingly, the MAC3B WD phenotype more closely resembles the MAC3A decoy phenotype, suggesting that MAC3A and MAC3B may have diverged slightly in their biochemical function or oligomerization capabilities.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing phenotypes.

claims.claim: Oligomerization plays an important role in MAC3B function in the clock.
claims.source: This was different than expressing the decoy or full-length MAC3B and indicates that oligomerization plays an important role in MAC3B function in the clock.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the MAC3B WD data.

results.result: The authors establish that few E3 ubiquitin ligases regulating the circadian clock have been identified due to high functional redundancy in plant E3 ligase families, particularly in Arabidopsis where gene expansion has created ~700 F-box genes compared to 69 in humans. This redundancy makes traditional forward genetic approaches inefficient, motivating the development of reverse genetic strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C27-C34 collectively establish the scientific rationale for the study. The claims are well-supported by citations (C29-C31, C33) and represent established knowledge in the field. The inference that redundancy hampers traditional genetics (C28, C32, C34) is reasonable given the cited evidence of gene expansion and semi-dominant alleles.

results.result: The decoy approach involves expressing E3 ubiquitin ligases lacking E2-recruiting ability but retaining substrate-binding capacity, acting as dominant-negatives that inactivate endogenous ligases and stabilize substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 describe the decoy methodology with appropriate citations (C35, C36). The mechanism is clearly articulated and supported by prior work. This establishes the technical foundation for the screening approach used in the study.

results.result: A library of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing decoy E3 ubiquitin ligases was successfully generated, covering nearly 1/4 of Arabidopsis E3 ligases across 16 protein-protein interaction domain classes. The library achieved 82% cloning success for F-box genes with 65% transgenic plant recovery, and 65% coverage of the U-box family, with diverse domain representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C39-C58 describe the library construction with specific quantitative metrics shown in Figures 1b-c. The success rates are reasonable for large-scale cloning projects and the domain distribution data appears comprehensive. The library represents a substantial technical achievement and resource for the community.

results.result: The decoy screen identified dozens of potential circadian regulators, with a surprisingly large number showing minor effects and a smaller number showing dramatic effects on clock period or phase. Only 5 individual plants showed arrhythmicity (RAE >0.6) compared to 0 in controls, and no decoy population had more than one arrhythmic plant.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C41-C42, and C59-C61 summarize the overall screening results with quantitative data from Figures 2-3. The observation that no decoy ablates clock function entirely (C61) is important for interpreting the results. The data support the conclusion that many E3 ligases have subtle effects on clock function.

results.result: Most decoy populations showed a ~1 hr phase advance attributed to general transgene expression effects. After accounting for this, 40 F-box decoy populations (22% of tested) showed statistically significant phase changes, with 37 having minor effects (<2 hr) and 3 having major effects (>2 hr). Three U-box populations also showed phase differences, all minor.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C72 describe phase analysis results with appropriate statistical testing (Bonferroni-corrected Welch's t-test) shown in Figures 4-5. The recognition of a general transgene effect (C63) and the statistical approach to account for it strengthen the analysis. The quantitative thresholds for major vs. minor effects are clearly defined.

results.result: Three F-box genes with major phase effects (ACF1, ACF2, CFK1) were characterized using public databases. ACF1 and ACF2 have close homologs and no prior functional studies. CFK1 has been studied, shows light-induced expression, interacts with the COP9 signalosome, and has a close homolog CFK2 with partial redundancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C88 provide bioinformatic characterization of candidate genes using cited databases and literature (Table 1). The analysis appropriately identifies homologs that could explain why these genes weren't found in forward screens. The CFK1 data (C84-C88) from prior literature provides supporting evidence for its potential clock role.

results.result: 36 F-box decoy populations (19% of tested) showed significantly different periods, with only one having a major effect (AT1G20800, 1.02 hr longer). Two populations showed distinct subpopulations with different period effects. Only 3 of 41 identified populations/subpopulations had shorter periods than wildtype.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C100 describe period analysis with appropriate statistics (Bonferroni-corrected Welch's t-test) and custom MATLAB analysis for subpopulation detection shown in Figure 6. The subpopulation analysis is innovative and the traces in Figure 7 support the quantitative findings. The predominance of long-period effects is an interesting biological observation.

results.result: Three F-box genes with major period effects (ACF3, ACF4, ACF5) were characterized. All have close homologs and limited prior characterization. ACF3 and ACF4 show no circadian/diurnal regulation, while ACF5 has no available expression data.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C110 provide bioinformatic analysis of period-regulating candidates using databases (Table 2). The identification of close homologs for all three genes supports the hypothesis that redundancy prevented their discovery in forward screens. The lack of prior characterization makes these novel candidates.

results.result: Two U-box decoy populations showed longer average periods (AT2G33340: 1.31 hr, AT5G62560: 0.37 hr), with AT2G33340 being the only U-box with a major effect. Three additional populations had subpopulations with period differences, including AT1G04510 with both long and short period subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C119 describe U-box period analysis with appropriate statistics shown in Figure 8. The identification of subpopulations with opposing effects (C118-C119) is particularly interesting. However, the authors note in Figure 9b that AT5G18340 (PUB48) shows some rhythmic abnormality requiring careful interpretation.

results.result: Two U-box genes with period effects (PUB30 and PUB48) were characterized. Both contain ARM repeats, have close homologs, show global expression, and are involved in stress responses (PUB30 in salt stress, PUB48 in drought stress). PUB48 shows rhythmic expression under circadian but not diurnal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C130 provide literature-based characterization of PUB30 and PUB48 (Table 3) with appropriate citations. The connection to stress responses is interesting given known links between stress and circadian function. The expression patterns support potential clock involvement.

results.result: MAC3A and MAC3B are 82% identical U-box proteins containing 7 WD repeats that act redundantly. They are orthologous to PRP19, a core component of the spliceosome activation machinery (NTC), and have established roles in splicing and miRNA biogenesis. Splicing is a critical regulatory step in plant clock function.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C139 establish the molecular identity and prior functional characterization of MAC3A/MAC3B with extensive citations (Table 3). The connection to splicing (C136-C139) provides a clear mechanistic hypothesis for their clock role. This background strongly motivates the detailed follow-up studies.

results.result: Single mac3a and mac3b mutants show minimal clock effects, but the double mutant exhibits significant phase delays (5.90 hr for CCA1, 3.95 hr for TOC1, though TOC1 not statistically significant). This demonstrates redundancy and identifies MAC3A/MAC3B as the first U-box genes regulating the circadian clock in any system.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C148 present genetic validation data from Figure 10 with appropriate statistical analysis (FFT-NLLS, Bonferroni correction). The lack of single mutant phenotypes (C140) combined with double mutant effects (C141-C143) definitively demonstrates redundancy (C148). The secondary TOC1 peak (C146) complicates interpretation but doesn't undermine the main conclusion. This is a key validation of the decoy approach.

results.result: The mac3a/mac3b mutant shows decreased amplitude of active PRR9 spliceoforms (PRR9a and PRR9b) and increased amplitude of the inactive intron-retaining form (PRR9c). This is consistent with the known role of another NTC component (SKIP) in regulating PRR9 splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C153 present splicing data from Figure 11A-C. While the trends are visible in the qRT-PCR data, the authors note in Figure 11D that large variability prevents statistical significance. The connection to SKIP (C150) provides supporting context, but the lack of statistical significance and limited analysis of other clock genes weakens the mechanistic conclusion. Additional validation would strengthen this result.

results.result: Constitutive overexpression of full-length MAC3B causes period lengthening similar to the mac3a/mac3b double mutant, indicating that proper MAC3B expression levels are necessary for clock function.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 present overexpression data from Figure 12 with appropriate citation support (C154). The observation that both loss and gain of function cause similar phenotypes (C155) is interesting and suggests a requirement for precise dosage. However, the mechanism underlying this observation requires further investigation.

results.result: The MAC3B decoy forms biologically relevant complexes in vivo, co-immunoprecipitating with five known NTC components including MAC3A, CDC5, and MOS4 (found only in MAC3B IP-MS, not controls). This validates the decoy approach for biochemical studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C160 present IP-MS data from Table 4 demonstrating that decoys retain complex-forming ability. The identification of known NTC components specifically in MAC3B IPs (C159) provides strong validation. This supports both the biological relevance of the decoy and the proposed mechanism involving the NTC complex.

results.result: MAC3A and MAC3B interact in IP-MS data, and their ortholog PRP19 forms tetramers via a conserved coiled-coil domain present in both proteins. Expression of MAC3B WD domain (lacking oligomerization region) produces two subpopulations with opposing period effects, resembling MAC3A decoy more than MAC3B decoy, suggesting oligomerization is important for MAC3B clock function and that MAC3A/MAC3B may have diverged in biochemical function.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C167 present domain analysis and functional dissection data from Figure 12. The MAC3A/MAC3B interaction (C161) and PRP19 tetramerization (C162-C164) are well-supported by citations. The MAC3B WD phenotype (C165) provides functional evidence for oligomerization importance (C167). The inference about functional divergence (C166) is reasonable but speculative.
